column1: How does radiation sensitivity differ between testicular germ cells (spermatogenesis) and Leydig cells (testosterone production)?
column2:
Germ cells are extraordinarily sensitive (damaged by >=0.1-1.2 Gy), whereas Leydig cells are much more radioresistant (tolerating up to 20-24 Gy before primary hypogonadism develops).

PDF p. 1009

column1: Why is lifelong surveillance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis required in survivors exposed to high-dose cranial radiation (>=40-50 Gy)?
column2:
Central ACTH deficiency can develop insidiously 10 to 15+ years after radiotherapy, predisposing survivors to fatal adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness.

PDF p. 1005

column1: At what pubertal stage is pubertal suppression with GnRH agonists officially recommended in transgender youth?
column2:
At the confirmed onset of biological puberty, defined as Tanner stage 2 (breast budding in AFAB; testicular volume >=4 mL in AMAB); it is not initiated in prepubertal children (Tanner 1).

PDF p. 1027

column1: How does the reversibility of GnRH agonist pubertal suppression compare with gender-affirming sex steroid therapy?
column2:
GnRH agonist pubertal suppression is fully reversible (endogenous puberty resumes if stopped), whereas gender-affirming sex steroid therapy induces partially irreversible changes (e.g., voice deepening, breast tissue).

PDF p. 1028

column1: What hematologic parameter must be monitored regularly in transgender males receiving testosterone therapy to prevent polycythemia?
column2:
Hemoglobin and hematocrit; testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis, and doses should be reduced if hematocrit exceeds 50-52%.

PDF p. 1033

column1: What are the therapeutic serum hormone targets for transgender females undergoing feminizing hormone therapy?
column2:
Serum 17-beta estradiol maintained between 100 and 200 pg/mL, with serum total testosterone suppressed to <50 ng/dL.

PDF p. 1031

column1: What electrolyte abnormality requires routine monitoring in transgender females taking spironolactone as an antiandrogen?
column2:
Hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), due to spironolactone's aldosterone-antagonist effect on the distal renal tubule.

PDF p. 1034

column1: When must counseling regarding fertility preservation options be conducted with transgender youth and their families?
column2:
Prior to initiating pubertal suppression (GnRHa) or gender-affirming hormone therapy (estrogen/testosterone), while gametogenesis is still intact.

PDF p. 1034

column1: Why is DXA bone mineral density monitoring indicated during prolonged GnRH agonist pubertal suppression?
column2:
Sex steroids are required for normal pubertal bone mineral accretion; prolonged gonadotropin suppression can delay peak bone mass acquisition, requiring calcium/vitamin D optimization.

PDF p. 1034

column1: What is the emergency intravenous hydrocortisone bolus dose for an acute adrenal crisis in children based on age?
column2:
<3 years: 25 mg; 3 to 12 years: 50 mg; >12 years: 100 mg IV bolus (or 50-100 mg/m2 IV), administered immediately alongside normal saline and dextrose.

PDF p. 1050

column1: Why must Lugol's iodine solution be given at least 1 hour AFTER methimazole when treating thyroid storm?
column2:
To ensure that methimazole has blocked thyroid peroxidase first; administering iodine before organification is blocked provides substrate that synthesizes more thyroid hormone (Jod-Basedow effect).

PDF p. 1054

column1: Why is aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) strictly contraindicated in the management of hyperpyrexia during thyroid storm?
column2:
Aspirin displaces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) from thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), sharply increasing free active thyroid hormone concentrations and worsening thyrotoxic storm.

PDF p. 1054

column1: Why is 10% calcium gluconate preferred over 10% calcium chloride for peripheral intravenous treatment of acute hypocalcemia?
column2:
Calcium chloride is highly irritating to veins and causes severe full-thickness tissue necrosis and sloughing if extravasation occurs; calcium gluconate carries a much lower tissue toxicity profile.

PDF p. 1056

column1: What is the immediate bedside pharmacological treatment for cerebral edema complicating pediatric DKA?
column2:
Intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg over 20 minutes) given immediately without awaiting imaging.

PDF p. 1046

column1: What is the emergency rescue dose of glucagon for severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious child with type 1 diabetes?
column2:
0.5 mg SC/IM for children <25 kg (or <6 years) and 1.0 mg SC/IM for children >=25 kg (or >=6 years); alternatively, 3 mg nasal glucagon for age >=4 years.

PDF p. 1048

column1: What is the first and most critical resuscitation step in the management of acute hypercalcemic crisis (calcium >14 mg/dL)?
column2:
Vigorous volume expansion with intravenous 0.9% normal saline at 2 to 3 times maintenance to restore renal perfusion and induce calciuresis.

PDF p. 1057

column1: What neuroendocrine distinction differentiates the acute phase of critical illness from the chronic phase in pediatric intensive care?
column2:
The acute phase features hypercortisolemia and sympathetic overdrive with adaptive downregulation of anabolic axes; the chronic phase features neuroendocrine exhaustion and persistent central anterior pituitary hypopituitarism.

PDF p. 1064

column1: What is the primary clinical presentation that prompts initiation of stress-dose hydrocortisone for suspected CIRCI in pediatric intensive care?
column2:
Vasopressor-refractory septic shock (persistent hypotension and poor perfusion requiring escalating doses of norepinephrine or epinephrine despite adequate fluid resuscitation).

PDF p. 1068

column1: What is the recommended empiric stress dosage of intravenous hydrocortisone for vasopressor-refractory pediatric septic shock?
column2:
50 mg/m2 (or 2 mg/kg) IV bolus, followed by 50 to 100 mg/m2/day as a continuous infusion or divided every 6 hours, tapered as vasopressors are weaned.

PDF p. 1071

column1: What blood glucose target range is internationally recommended for critically ill children in the PICU receiving insulin for stress hyperglycemia?
column2:
Moderate glycemic control targeting blood glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10.0 mmol/L), avoiding strict normoglycemia (80-110 mg/dL) due to high hypoglycemia risk.

PDF p. 1076

column1: What adverse complication was demonstrated in pediatric clinical trials (e.g., CHiP trial) evaluating tight glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL)?
column2:
A high incidence of severe iatrogenic hypoglycemia (<40 mg/dL), which caused secondary brain injury and increased adverse outcomes.

PDF p. 1076

column1: Is routine thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3) recommended for low T3/T4 levels in critically ill children?
column2:
No. Randomized trials show no clinical benefit in mortality or ICU length of stay, and guidelines recommend against routine replacement therapy.

PDF p. 1080

column1: What pattern of circulating growth hormone and IGF-1 characterizes the acute phase of critical illness?
column2:
Elevated circulating growth hormone accompanied by markedly depressed serum IGF-1 concentrations, reflecting acute peripheral hepatic growth hormone resistance.

PDF p. 1081
